content: The University of Buckingham is one of only two private universities in the United Kingdom, the other being Richmond University. The university operates two campuses in Buckingham, Buckinghamshire, located approximately 20 miles northeast of Oxford and 15 miles west of Milton Keynes. One campus primarily focuses on Law, while the riverside campus in the town center is dedicated to Business, Humanities, and Science. Notably, Buckingham is the only university in the UK that operates independently of direct government funding. Among its distinguished academics are philosopher Roger Scruton, educationalist Alan Smithers, historian John Adamson, biographer Jane Ridley, and former Chief Inspector of Schools Chris Woodhead. The university's origins trace back to the late 1960s, when some academics from the University of Oxford, dissatisfied with the prevailing ethos of the time, sought to establish a new institution. On May 27, 1967, Dr. J.W. Paulley published a letter in The Times proposing the creation of a university modeled after the great private foundations in the United States. This idea was further explored in three London conferences, leading to the incorporation of the University College of Buckingham in 1973. The institution received its Royal Charter in 1983. Its development was heavily influenced by the libertarian Institute of Economic Affairs, particularly through the efforts of Harry Ferns and Ralph Harris. Reflecting its libertarian philosophy, the university's foundation stone was laid by Margaret Thatcher, who later served as its Chancellor from 1993 to 1998. The first two Vice-Chancellors were Lord Beloff and Sir Alan Peacock, both prominent academics and libertarians. The main campus is situated in the historic county town of Buckingham, nestled within a bend of the River Ouse. It features a mix of seventeenth, eighteenth, and nineteenth-century buildings alongside modern teaching facilities. Some student residences are located directly along the river, offering scenic views. The historic Tanlaw Mill, adjacent to the river, serves as a social hub for students, housing bars, a gym, a café, and other amenities. The Clore Laboratory, a modern facility, is also located nearby, as is Yeomanry House on Hunter Street, which serves as the university's administrative center. The Antony de Rothschild Building, overlooking the river, houses the Department of International Studies and Economics. Across the river, the Chandos Building contains lecture theaters, language and media suites, exam halls, and gallery spaces. The university's second campus, located on a hill near the town's edge, features a central brick building that was formerly a convent. The University of Buckingham is organized into four main faculties: Law, Humanities, Business, and Science. It is particularly renowned for its tutorial-based teaching model, a tradition brought over from the University of Oxford. In addition to seminars and large lectures, much of the teaching occurs in small groups of four to eight students, allowing for a highly personalized educational experience. The university boasts a staff-to-student ratio of 1:10, placing it among the highest in the UK in this regard. Academic quality is maintained through an External Examiner system, an Academic Advisory Council, and adherence to the principles of the Quality Assurance Agency for Higher Education (QAA). Buckingham offers traditional degree programs but compresses the typical three-year curriculum into two years by requiring students to study for eight terms instead of nine. This accelerated format is considered cost-effective, as it reduces living expenses and allows students to enter the workforce a year earlier. As of September 2008, tuition fees for UK/EU undergraduate students were set at £6,030 per year, while non-EU students paid £10,125 annually. The university's research activities span several fields. In Law, it specializes in family law and gender-related legal studies. In Humanities, it focuses on Charles Dickens, particularly through the Dickens Journals Online (DJO) project, as well as biography and life-writing. In Business, the emphasis is on entrepreneurship, while in Science, research centers on diabetes, obesity, and metabolic studies at the Clore Laboratory, as well as face recognition systems in Computer Sciences. The Centre for Education and Employment Research, led by Alan Smithers and Dr. Pamela Robinson, conducts studies on the state of education for policymakers and practitioners. Their findings are frequently featured in national media. The Dickens Journals Online project aims to provide free access to a complete digital edition of Dickens's weekly magazines, offering a rich resource of nineteenth-century literature, opinion, and history. The Denning Law Journal, edited by Professor Susan Edwards, is another notable academic output from the university. The University of Buckingham was established as a liberal arts college in the tradition of North American Ivy League institutions. It offers major humanities subjects such as History and Politics, often combined with Economics in its International Studies degree. Economics is also available as a standalone degree, as are English Literature and Journalism-related combined degrees. Professor Martin Ricketts, the Dean of Humanities and Professor of Economics, chairs the Academic Advisory Council of the Institute of Economic Affairs, reinforcing the university's libertarian connections. The largest school within the university is the School of Law, followed by Humanities, Business Studies, and Accounting. Some science departments, such as Biology, focus exclusively on research degrees, while others, like Psychology and Computer Sciences, offer a full range of undergraduate and postgraduate programs. The School of Law has been recognized as a flagship program, achieving a top-20 ranking in the Guardian league tables out of 90 law schools in the UK. The university maintains international partnerships, including with the Sarajevo School of Science and Technology in Bosnia. It has also established a postgraduate medical school under the leadership of Professor Karol Sikora, with the first intake for the MD in Clinical Medicine expected in September 2008. The Department of Education includes prominent figures such as Professor Chris Woodhead, Professor Anthony O'Hear, and Professor Alan Smithers. Its Postgraduate Certificate in Education (PGCE), which specializes in the independent sector, has recently been accredited for Qualified Teacher Status (QTS), enabling graduates to teach in state schools. Notable alumni of the University of Buckingham include Richard Ballerand, Bader Ben Hirsi, Susanne Klatten, Brandon Lewis, and Olagunsoye Oyinlola. In popular culture, John Lloyd, host of the BBC Radio 4 program The Museum of Curiosity, humorously refers to himself as The Professor of Ignorance at the University of Buckingham. During the 1980s, author V.M. Xavier presented special cultural performances at student events. The university also awards undergraduate and postgraduate degrees, including MBAs, to students studying at the European School of Economics. The current Chancellor is Sir Martin Jacomb, who holds prominent positions in several organizations, including Canary Wharf Group PLC and Oxford Playhouse Trust. He previously served as Chairman of Prudential PLC and was a board member of Rio Tinto PLC and Marks & Spencer PLC. Former Chancellors include Margaret Thatcher and Lord Hailsham of St Marylebone. The current Vice-Chancellor, Dr. Terence Kealey, has held the position since April 2001 and is a noted academic specializing in Clinical Biochemistry. The University of Buckingham Press publishes scholarly works in the fields of law, education, and business, including journal articles, books, and reports.
